explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, asks, “Should he argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose?” (Job 15:3). So he is calling Job's speeches empty. That's a rough review, and I'd be hiding behind my mixing bowl right about now.

Not quite, friend. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, calls Job's talk “empty counsel” and compares it to filling his belly with “the hot east wind.” Nothing about that sounds gentle. Hot wind is the opposite of a soft pat on the shoulder.

Close, but length never comes up. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, asks about “useless words or speeches that serve no purpose” (Job 15:3). His complaint is that they accomplish nothing, however long they run. I think even a short speech gets that review if Eliphaz thinks it's empty.

That's the one, baker. Eliphaz says, “Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you.” He is pointing at what Job has said. Eliphaz wants everybody to know that the words are Job's, and Eliphaz just happens to be standing there.

Hands never show up in this line, friend. Eliphaz says, “Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you.” His whole point is about Job's words, not anything Job did with his hands. Hands are busy enough in my bakery without getting blamed for this.

Feet aren't in this verse, baker. Eliphaz says, “Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you.” Both of those are about speaking. Nobody is getting called out for where they walked.

That's his point, baker. Eliphaz asks, “What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?” (Job 15:9). Before that he asks whether Job listens in on God's council or limits wisdom to himself. He is saying Job has no secret knowledge. It's a bold thing to say to a man in Job's spot.

explanations.answer: Job is older than all of them
explanations.explanation: Other way around, friend. Eliphaz says the gray-haired and the aged are on their side, “men much older than your father” (Job 15:10). He isn't making Job the oldest in the room. He is saying he has some of the oldest folks backing him up.

Praying isn't what Eliphaz brings up here. He asks, “What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?” (Job 15:9). He is questioning whether Job knows anything beyond what they know. The question is about knowledge, not how often anyone prays.

True, baker. Eliphaz says, “Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side—men much older than your father.” He is lining up a whole row of elders behind him. I think he wants Job to feel outnumbered by experience.

It's true, friend. Eliphaz says, “Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side—men much older than your father.” So the elders he mentions are older than Job's own father. He is not saying they're younger or the same age. That's a lot of birthdays standing behind him.

You got it, baker. Eliphaz asks why Job's heart has carried him away and why his eyes flash, “so that you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?” (Job 15:12-13). That's what he accuses Job of. Those are Eliphaz's words about Job, and they land hard.
Hiding isn't in this verse, friend. Eliphaz asks why Job's heart has carried him away and why his eyes flash. Flashing eyes are the opposite of hiding. He says Job is turning his spirit against God.

Running away isn't what Eliphaz says. He says Job's heart has carried him away and his eyes flash, “so that you turn your spirit against God.” Turning against someone is a different thing from running from them. Eliphaz is describing Job as facing God, not fleeing Him.

Other way around, baker. Eliphaz says, “If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes…” (Job 15:15). So he says God puts no trust in them, not complete trust. Eliphaz is using that to make a point about man.

That's right, friend. Eliphaz says, “If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes…” (Job 15:15). He says God puts no trust in them, the opposite of complete trust. He then asks how much less man could measure up.

That's it, baker. Eliphaz says man is “vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water” (Job 15:16). That's a picture of someone gulping it down without a second thought. It's a heavy way for Eliphaz to talk about people.
Kindness would be a whole different speech, friend. Eliphaz says man is “vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water.” The word is injustice. Kindness doesn't show up anywhere in this line.

Wisdom is close to what this speech keeps talking about, baker, but it's not the answer here. Eliphaz says man is “vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water” (Job 15:16). The thing being gulped down is injustice. Wisdom is what he claims for himself.

You got it, baker. Eliphaz says, “A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless.” (Job 15:20). He opens his teaching with the wicked man and stays on him to the end of the speech. Everything after this is what Eliphaz says happens to him.

Not this time, friend. Eliphaz begins with “A wicked man writhes in pain all his days…” (Job 15:20). The teaching is about the wicked, not a faithful servant. That's who he is describing from here to the end.

No widow in this speech, baker. Eliphaz says, “A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless.” (Job 15:20). The wicked man is the one in the spotlight. Nobody else gets a turn in this part.

Careful with this one, baker. Eliphaz says, “in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him” (Job 15:21). So the attack comes while the man is prosperous, not when he's poor. Eliphaz has the order flipped from what this question says.

That's right, friend. Eliphaz says, “Sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him.” The attack comes in his prosperity, not after he's poor. So the trouble arrives while things look good.

explanations.answer: Stretched out his hand against God
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Eliphaz says, “For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty” (Job 15:25). That's the reason he gives for the trouble. He puts it all on the man's stance toward God.

Offerings never come up here, friend. Eliphaz says the wicked man “has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty” (Job 15:25). That's the whole reason he gives. Nothing about skipped offerings.

Servants aren't mentioned, baker. Eliphaz says the wicked man “has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty” (Job 15:25). His charge is about how the man treats God. This verse doesn't say anything about servants.

True, baker. Eliphaz says the wicked man is “rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield” (Job 15:26). That's a charging picture, and he's carrying heavy protection. It's the picture Eliphaz paints of someone running at the Almighty.
It's true, friend. Eliphaz says the wicked man is “rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield” (Job 15:26). So he's pictured rushing at God, shield and all. This verse really does say it.

That's the word, baker. Eliphaz says the wicked man “will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble” (Job 15:28). It's a picture of a man ending up in a broken-down place. Nobody is renting there.

Royal sounds fancy, friend, but that's not the word. Eliphaz says the wicked man “will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.” Rubble is about as far from a palace as you can get. The word is ruined.

Holy doesn't fit this line, baker. Eliphaz says the wicked man “will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.” These are broken-down places, nothing sacred about them. The word is ruined.

Other way around, baker. Eliphaz says, “He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure.” (Job 15:29). So the wealth doesn't last. He also says the man's possessions will not overspread the land.

That's right, friend. Eliphaz says, “He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure. His possessions will not overspread the land.” (Job 15:29). So the wealth doesn't last. Eliphaz says none of it sticks around.

You got it, baker. Eliphaz says, “Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward.” (Job 15:31). The word shows up twice, and he means it both times. Trust in empty things, and empty is what you get.

Riches aren't the reward here, friend. Eliphaz says, “Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward.” (Job 15:31). The reward is emptiness. Earlier he even says the man's wealth will not endure (Job 15:29).

Honor isn't on the list, baker. Eliphaz says, “Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward.” (Job 15:31). The reward is emptiness, not a trophy or a title. That's the whole warning.

That's his point, baker. Eliphaz says, “his branch will not flourish” and then pictures “a vine stripped of its unripe grapes” and “an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.” (Job 15:32-33). Both pictures show something that loses what it needs to bear fruit. That's the image he gives of the wicked man.

No comeback story here, friend. Eliphaz says, “his branch will not flourish,” and the vine and olive tree are losing what they would grow. A vine stripped of grapes and an olive tree shedding blossoms (Job 15:33) aren't headed anywhere good. Eliphaz isn't promising a bounce back.

Feeding folks isn't the picture, baker. Eliphaz says, “his branch will not flourish,” and his vine and olive tree are losing what they would produce. Grapes stripped off and blossoms shed (Job 15:33) don't turn into a big harvest. Eliphaz is describing someone who ends up with nothing to give.

That's the word, baker. Eliphaz says, “They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit.” (Job 15:35). He pictures trouble starting and evil coming out of it. That's how he ends the speech.
Peace would be a nice twist, friend, but that's not what Eliphaz says. He says, “They conceive trouble and give birth to evil.” (Job 15:35). Trouble in, evil out. Peace doesn't come into it.

Mercy would be lovely, baker, but it isn't in this line. Eliphaz says, “They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit.” (Job 15:35). The word is evil. Eliphaz saves his last line for a hard picture of the godless.
